utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-00-39-A, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I will now call for the appearances of the parties and of the amicus. The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCCALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Shelagh McCall is my name. The counsel beside me is Peter Kremer and with us our case manager, Lourdes Galicia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. McCall.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I am Colin Nicholls, acting as amicus curiae and I am assisted by Ms. Michelle Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Krajisnik, can you hear the proceedings in a language that you understand? THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Yes. I do understand, Your Honour. Thank you very much. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. You may be seated. This, as you know, is a Status Conference called in accordance with Rule 65 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Rule 65 bis(B) requires a Status Conference to be convened within 120 days of the last Status Conference to allow any person in custody, pending appeal, the opportunity to raise issues in relation thereto, including the mental and physical condition of this person. The last Status Conference in this case was held on 5 April 2007. I would like to begin this Status Conference by inquiring into Mr. Krajisnik's health. Mr. Krajisnik, I would like you to respond on this issue. Any problems with your health to which you would like to alert me? THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] No problems, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm glad to hear that. In a moment, I will give you a chance to address other issues, if you have any, but right now I wanted to limit myself to this question of any concerns about your mental or physical well being and I'm glad to hear that there are none. Before I turn to other issues I want to say a few words to the parties and to the amicus about scheduling. I'm sure you're all aware of how the schedule works but I want to go through it again now. First, on the Prosecution appeal. The briefing on this was completed on the 22nd of February 2007 when the Prosecution filed its reply brief and so I believe we are all set in regards to this. Second, in relation to the appeal of Mr. Krajisnik, based on our decision of 11 May, we have two sets of deadlines going on. With regard to the amicus, the notice of appeal has been filed. The appeal brief is due 75 days after 11 May, which, by my calculation, would be July 25. After that, we follow our usual deadlines in accordance with Rules 112 and 113. With regard to Mr. Krajisnik, the notice of appeal has also been filed and the appeal brief is due 75 days after the translation of the judgement into B/C/S. The B/C/S translation of the judgement will hopefully be ready shortly, and Mr. Krajisnik's appeal brief will be due 75 days after that. The Prosecution's response will be due within the usual time frame after that, and Mr. Krajisnik's reply will be due within 15 days of when he receives the B/C/S translation of the Prosecution's response. This case has progressed slowly so far, partly in light of the Appeals Chamber consideration and the resolution of Mr. Krajisnik's request to self-represent himself. In light of the slow pace, I will be particularly reluctant to grant any motions that will have the effect of delaying the proceedings further. And I trust and expect the parties to meet all the deadlines. Mr. Krajisnik, I would like to say to you in particular that the Appeals Chamber has acceded to your argument that you have the right of self-representation, and as you know, I myself was one of the Judges in the majority who supported this conclusion, but, of course, we expect you to conduct your appeal in a professional manner and to abide by the requirements set out in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and in the relevant practice directions, including with regard to word counts, to precise arguments in support of your grounds of appeal, with specific references to the judgement below and the relevant evidence and to other rights. We are undoubtedly on the same page, on the same wave length in hoping that your exercise of your right to self-representation will lead to no disruption of the appeal proceeding. Failure to abide by the rules, in particular those pertaining to deadlines, may lead to substantial and persistent disruption of the case and might have -- and might give cause for the Appeals Chamber to revisit your self-representation. And I wanted, Mr. Krajisnik, to be very clear in all fairness to you at this stage about my approach to these issues. In this regard, Mr. Krajisnik, I note that you recently filed a request to provide conditions to work and to reverse the decision of the Registry of 7 June 2007 with the Appeals Chamber. I will not make much comment on this motion as it is pending before the Appeals Chamber, but I will note that in my view, the Prosecution pointed out already some ways in which this motion failed to comply with the practice directions such as by filing -- failing to give -- by failing to give a word count and by failing to provide precise citations to specific paragraphs and/or to pages of the documents referenced. Mr. Krajisnik, I trust that this was an oversight and that this will not happen again. I hope very much that your self-representation will not disrupt or obstruct an orderly appeal process. At this point I would like to ask the parties and amicus whether they have any other issues they would like to raise at this time. Ms. McCall?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCCALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. One matter arises out of what you have just said and it's this: This morning the Prosecution filed a motion requesting clarification of one or two matters arising from the 11th May decision and one of those issues relates to the calculation of time limits for filings. And the Prosecution is seeking a standing ruling from the Appeals Chamber that the deadline for Prosecution filings in response to those by Mr. Krajisnik will not start to run until the English translation of his filing is received. So when Your Honour this morning said that the Prosecution's response to his appeal brief would be due in the usual time frame after filing of his brief, that causes us some concern because his brief will of course be filed in B/C/S and we will have to wait for the English translation. But that's a matter that can perhaps be considered by the Chamber in discussing the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I will be -- if you trust my approach to this, I would be prepared to clarify this matter now for the parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCCALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Then that will deal with one aspect of the motion we filed this morning. The rest doesn't arise today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I would like to clarify to both the Prosecution and Mr. Krajisnik -- Mr. Krajisnik you may be seated. Did you want to say anything at this stage or -- thank you. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: The deadline for Mr. Krajisnik apply to the B/C/S versions of his appeal brief and his reply brief. The Prosecution's clock for its response will not start running until it receives the English translation of Mr. Krajisnik's appeal brief. I hope that this clarifies this matter. And as regards Mr. Krajisnik, let me make it quite clear, that when we say that Mr. Krajisnik's brief is due 75 days after the B/C/S translation of the judgement, we mean, of course, that his B/C/S appeal brief is due then, not the English translation. Otherwise, he would have to work to a much tighter schedule to allow time for translation. The same logic would apply to his reply brief subsequently. Okay. Do you have any other questions or comments, Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCCALL
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. So I'm glad we could clarify this and I hope that both parties are pleased with this approach. Now, I turn to Mr. Krajisnik. Now you may stand up. And ask you whether you have any matters that you would like to raise with me as Pre-Appeal Judge in this case. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Judge, first of all, I would like to thank you and the Appeals Chamber for making it possible for me to represent myself. I assure you that I will do my very best, and I certainly know I can, to abide by your deadlines and not to abuse in any way your decision which is so important for me. There is one thing I do have to ask you. Since my brief will not be discussed today, could it please be made possible for me technically and financially to be able to carry through that decision of yours? There is nothing else I'm asking for. I am sorry and I'm trying to find an excuse now for not having acted appropriately within the rules and not having filed this brief. I certainly would need a bit of help on that, and that has to do with some of the points contained in this brief. I am sorry, Judge, that I had to address you and the Appeals Chamber for assistance because without certain assistance - I am in prison, after all - I cannot really carry through this decision without some assistance. I am in prison, after all, and it really only depends on technical matters, and thank you once again for having found it expedient to allow me to represent myself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I am confident in believing that the Registry would assist you on some vital technical and financial matters, but those requests that you are submitting to the Registry must fit into the existing rules and requirements. For example, things are being delayed because of problems pertaining to your legal associates, yet you must understand that those legal associates that you would like to have must fit into the existing rules. We have a rule regarding qualifications, and I have been -- I understand that so far, you have not suggested, for example, names of people who could start helping you, and I understand you need this help, and who have met the requirements of the Registry with regard to qualifications. So I would like this really to start moving. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Judge, not a single one of my requests is unfounded. None of the things I ask for in my brief, that is. Believe me, every time I made proposals that met the requirements of Article 45, in one particular case it was necessary for the Registrar to use his discretionary right but he did not accept that. In another case, nothing else was needed but for them to accept a particular proposal. For me to be able to engage someone, apart from these rules, I need resources. They said that they would grant resources automatically once the Seselj case is resolved. The Seselj case was resolved yesterday and I believe that there will be no problem whatsoever in engaging, how should I put this, an adviser who would please them because nobody else met their requirements. I also asked for a translator who would work with me on the appeal. At first Mr. Nicholls was opposed to that as well and then the Registry too because I did not have a decision stating that I can represent myself. Later on there were some other difficulties too, clarification was sought, so there has been a delay on this count as well. I need a translator in order to be able to respond to briefs filed by the Prosecution. I could not read any one of them because they are in the English language. Therefore I understand your objection, but believe me, if this were on our agenda today I would have explained it to you how things developed but I did say so in my reply and I believe that this will be resolved in the next few days, though. Because resources have been granted to Mr. Seselj and they said we will automatically grant resources to you for your legal advisers so that you can pay them because nobody is willing to work without money. I found these people who would work at cheap rates and I could finance them myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, let me start from what is I think a relatively simple matter and it is the question of the translator. You have, if I understand correctly, asked the Registry to pay for and provide privileged access to a particular named individual, and the registry is not currently satisfied that this individual will abide by regulations in place for the safety and security of the detention centre. I am not aware of the Registry having declined in general to provide you with privileged access to a paid interpreter as opposed to declining to accept this specific interpreter you requested. I think that I would like to emphasise at this stage that it is really in your interest to work productively with the Registry to ensure the speedy and appropriate progress of your appeal. I do not wish to revisit the question of your right to self-representation but you know that our precedents provide that this right may be removed in the face of substantial and persistent obstruction to the proper and expeditious course of the proceedings. So in this case, in particular, the fact that there are problems with Mr. Karganovic on whom you have insisted does not mean that the Registry is not willing to accommodate your reasonable claim to a paid interpreter or translator. So this is an example of the problems that have arisen. Now, as regards funding in general, you are aware of paragraph 18 of our decision of 11 May 2007. The Appeals Chamber made it clear that as part of the choice to self-represent, you, Mr. Krajisnik, must accept responsibility for the disadvantages that this choice necessarily may bring. If you choose to have counsel and you qualify for the indigency status, then the Registry would have provided you with counsel and some support for counsel. If you choose to self-represent, however, then the Registry has taken the position that you are not entitled to funding. I believe that the Registry has made its position clear in its letters of 29 May and 7 June. I don't want to second-guess the Registry but I would like also to note that in the absence of any appropriately designated legal associates, the question of what resources might be available to such associates is currently still a hypothetical question. You have still not named those associates which meets the -- passes the muster of the Registry. Let's just get on and not create unnecessary difficulties. I'm sure that you can come up with suggestions regarding legal associates who would not encounter these difficulties. We have rules on these matters. We have Rule 44 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. We must comply with them. I am telling -- saying those things in a good spirit, Mr. Krajisnik. I would like this experiment in self-representation on the appeal level to succeed. As you know, this was a controversial question and I think that you understand that rights -- and I've supported your right -- always involve obligations. They involve difficulties. You wanted that route. You have chosen it. We will try to make your task as reasonably easy as possible, but, please, don't create difficulties that need not arise. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Judge, by your leave, please, since the brief was not on our agenda, I did not explain this. I am not asking for anything that is outside the rules. I did not ask for money. I have reconciled myself to the fact that according to the rules, I do not have money. However, if there is an opportunity to obtain money, that will be apart from the rules. And then I found some proposals made by people who were prepared to work and be paid by me. I gave you an example. That was Mr. Dejan Brashich. Then, they told me that there was a difficulty involved because there were certain obstacles. Then I made yet another proposal. May I proceed, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Well, I really would not like to, as I told you, micromanage the discussions -- THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- with the Registry. I would like to leave those things, as far as possible, in the sphere of discussions between you and the registry. But please bear in mind the constraints explained to you under the rules by the Registry with regard to your potential legal associates. One should distinguish between the question of privileged access and the question of funding. You have decided to go the route of self-representation. There would have been no difficulties in funding had you, as most people, most defendants, have chosen the route of having a counsel. He would have been assigned to you, he would have been paid, he would have been given some legal assistance, but we cannot create new rules just for you, Mr. Krajisnik. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Judge, Judge, I will be very brief. I'm just asking you for one thing and that's where I need your assistance. For them not to prevent me from carrying through my decision, not to hinder the implementation of my decision. If I cannot use a telephone, a fax, a photocopier, if I make three proposals and none of them are good, then there is a problem. It is very hard to find a legal adviser who will -- well, there isn't much of a choice, is there? So I asked that my brief, my submission, be looked at and I explained every one of my proposals. Mr. Karganovic is directly here in the audience. He was not contested until two weeks ago. What was in dispute was the fact that there was no decision for me to represent myself. So all the proposals I make seem to be controversial. I said just resolve the problem. I don't mind if you assign your own interpreter or translator, doesn't matter, but I encounter problems all the time. I'm not asking for money. I'm not asking for anything outside the rules. I am just asking for it to be made possible for me to defend myself even in this position. I am going to write an appeal and lodge it in this Court, but, please, within everything that is allowed from the point of view of safety, security, status and everything, I'm not asking for anything else. I'm just asking for your assistance on that score. I'm not asking for any privileges and I'm not asking for anything apart from the rules, and I don't want to drag my feet on this. On the contrary. I want this to be done and over with as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. I do not believe that the Registry is trying to make your task more difficult than it is already. You have a difficult task, and we will keep our eyes and ears open on what is going on. As I told you, I don't want to get involved in that beyond the point that I have already -- the points that I have already made. But I have -- I understand that there is perhaps a different way of seeing the problems with regard to your proposed interpreter. I am -- I must tell you, rather impatient with regard to your naming legal associates. I understand that the Registry agreed to three legal associates but they must meet the qualifications. So let's not go around and around that. You have an obligation to assist in the process and to -- not to complicate the process by proposing individuals who create -- who are difficult for the -- or impossible for the Registry to accept. Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik, and I really wish that we would see fast progress, and please remember especially what I said about the deadlines. We are quite adamant that they should be adhered to. Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I correct one matter straight away which was said by Mr. Krajisnik? I do not object to the appointment of a translator, interpreter, or indeed to Mr. Karganovic. I have no standing in the matter as amicus and so I don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The second matter is one which I raise with some reluctance because I appreciate very much the importance of the timetable which the Chamber has determined. But we in our team are having some difficulties in achieving the deadline which has been imposed for the appeal brief. That is the date of the 25th of July. And I would hesitatingly ask that the Chamber would grant us a further nine days. That is comparatively not a long time, but the reason is this: Your Honour will recall that on the 25th of May, the Chamber determined that the amicus should not be granted an extension beyond the 25th of July, which had been fixed in fact in the decision of the 11th of July, and that refusal of extra time was of course communicated to me before I accepted the assignment of amicus. So in accepting the assignment of amicus, I appreciated the deadline that was being imposed and Your Honour will appreciate that of course I was very reluctant to decline the appointment of amicus because obviously of the disruption that it would cause to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And I appreciate your accepting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour for that. The difficulty is this: That that decision not to give us the extra time was made on the 25th of May and it might have been hoped that I could be assigned immediately after that but, in fact, it wasn't a question of negotiation or anything of that kind. It was not until the 8th of June that I was in fact assigned as amicus and it was a week later, on the 15th of June, that I was able to have my team assigned. That meant that I had lost effectively another three weeks before either I or my team were able to recommence work. So the situation had changed between the ruling of the 25th of May and the date of the 15th of June, in that the period in which my team was not able to work had been prolonged. Now, in addition to that, as always happens, there are a lot of administrative matters that have to be dealt with. One matter was that we had to arrange for a large quantity of documents, held at the beach house, to be transported to the prison for Mr. Krajisnik's benefit. That meant that they had to be inspected, that we had to try to make some arrangements for their removal and reception, and that inevitably in spite of what assistance the Registry was able to give us and UNDU was able to give us, it was a prolonged process. It has now been achieved to this extent that those documents, I say 152 boxes, will in fact be transported, as I understand it, to the prison today. But that took time and took time on the part of my team, who could have been drafting the documents and doing the necessary work on the reply. In addition to that, there was material which we had in London which had been part of the trial material, and that material had to be -- well, we initially put it on a hard drive and I don't want to go into technicalities but the hard drive was not acceptable to the authorities and we lost some four days burning DVDs in order that that material could be made available to Mr. Krajisnik. That material is now here and we are able to make it available to him today. So those documents are now due to reach him, but actually having to administer that process has lost us time, and time, as i say, in addition to the three weeks that we had lost following the ruling refusing us extra time on the 25th of May. So we having lost that time, I feel bound -- and I say with great reluctance I feel bound to ask the Chamber to grant an extra nine days. Now, the question of course that arises is what is the effect of that upon the subsequent deadlines? Does everything shift on another nine days? And I think that it may be that there is no real prejudice. If there is any prejudice, and indeed if it's appropriate I invite and indeed the Prosecution would respond in any event, but if there is any prejudice, I think it will be a prejudice to Mr. Krajisnik, which of course is the most important prejudice of all, in that he would get a copy of our appeal brief nine days later than he otherwise would have done. Now, in the current circumstances, and bearing in mind the enormous burden which falls upon Mr. Krajisnik, and it is an enormous burden, self-imposed as it may be, bearing in mind that, it may not really be a real prejudice, having regard to the fact that he's got to get acquainted with the papers, got to get acquainted with the case, beyond his current acquaintance with it. So far as the Prosecution is concerned, it may not affect possibly their deadlines, in that they would in fact be responding probably, possibly, on a consolidated basis, I don't know. As I say, I'm very, very reluctant to make this request but with the greatest will in the world, we are facing this difficulty. We want to make this an appeal brief which is understandable not only to the Chamber and the lawyers but we want to make it understandable, as best we can, to Mr. Krajisnik, and in order to do that, obviously we have to give extra time in order to make it properly accessible to him. As I say, I say this very reluctantly. I just have to make the request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. I would like to ask the Prosecution whether they have comments on this request for a for a five -- for a nine-day delay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCCALL
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has no objection to that proposal because the Prosecution recognises, as Mr. Nicholls points out, that it doesn't impact on the end date of the briefing schedule, the last filing being that of Mr. Krajisnik rather than that of the amicus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So in your view, this should not affect the filing schedule for Mr. Krajisnik should I grant the motion?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCCALL
utterances.text: Our position is that we don't oppose Your Honour granting the motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: No. But my question was: Do you suggest this would have an impact on the filing dates established for Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCCALL
utterances.text: As a proposal is set out, I don't understand what that impact would be because Mr. Krajisnik will inevitably be filing his brief after the amicus even with the extra nine days so he will be able to see what is contained in that. As I understand the 11th May decision, Mr. Krajisnik doesn't have a right of response to the amicus brief. The amicus standing, as it were, also in his shoes, so Mr. Krajisnik's reply will be the last filing in the briefing schedule and that would be unaffected by an extension for the amicus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nicholls, what I would suggest we do -- you do --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: -- is submit to me as a Pre-Appeal Judge a motion requesting for the reasons you have indicated, the nine-day delay and I will give it due consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Is there anything else you would have wanted to raise at this stage, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. There are no other matters at this stage, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So I think that this Status Conference can now come to its end. We have had a conversation with Mr. Krajisnik and explained the situation to him, and he has had an opportunity to make comments on the various aspects of the issues that we have before us, and I thank you, Mr. Krajisnik, for your cooperation. I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Judge, if I may have a moment, please, a new fact has been brought forward. I agree that Mr. Nicholls should be given an extra nine days. I believe that this would be beneficial, that would be of some use for me, and as far as the archives are concerned, since I don't have any room to accommodate the archives in the prison, I would kindly request for an authorised representative of mine to be handed over the archives. I'm talking about vast materials that would create a lot of problems in the Detention Unit. Let me explain why. My associates that will be working with me will be able to use the archives that will be outside the prison and I will be able to use the archives that I have in -- on my premises and that would be useful. This much for me, and I would like to thank you very much again for your patience and assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: For reasons which are nobody's fault, you don't have a legal associate as yet so let's speed that aspect up. As regards the space for you in the Detention Unit for those archives, I'm sure that you are making this point to the representatives of the Registry, and I would like to hope that on this point, reasonable accommodation can be -- could be found. I see your point on that. THE APPELLANT: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other comments? If not, we have completed this Status Conference, and I am -- I really would like to say I want this case to move on without any undue delays and I am counting on everybody, including of course, you, Mr. Krajisnik, to help us with that. We will now rise.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
